entities.name: hazard analysis and critical control points
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points (HACCP) represents a paradigm shift in food safety protocols, originating in the United States during the 1960s and gaining global traction in the following decades. Developed by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) in collaboration with Pillsbury, HACCP was initially created to ensure the safety of food for astronauts, thus underscoring the importance of systematic preventive approaches to food safety. As food production expanded and global supply chains became more intricate, HACCP emerged as a fundamental framework that transcended national boundaries and regulatory environments, reshaping food safety practices worldwide.

The HACCP framework is built upon seven core principles, including conducting hazard analyses, identifying critical control points, and establishing critical limits for each point. Its application has led to significant improvements in food safety standards, with countries adopting HACCP-based regulations to mitigate risks associated with biological, chemical, and physical hazards. By the late 1990s, HACCP had been endorsed by numerous international bodies, including the World Health Organization (WHO) and the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), further solidifying its role in global food safety governance.

The legacy of HACCP has been profound, influencing food safety legislation and practices across various sectors, including agriculture, food processing, and catering. Countries around the world have implemented HACCP protocols, resulting in a measurable decrease in foodborne illnesses and outbreaks. The principles of HACCP have also paved the way for modern food safety systems that prioritize preventive measures over reactive ones, demonstrating a significant shift in how societies approach public health and safety in food production.

Their legacy is studied through the lens of historical causation.", "summary": "Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points (HACCP) is a systematic preventive food safety management system that identifies, evaluates, and controls hazards (biological, chemical, physical) significant to food safety throughout the food production process — from raw material production through processing, distribution, and consumption. HACCP was developed jointly by the Pillsbury Company, the US Army Natick Laboratories, and NASA in the late 1950s–1960s as part of NASA's requirement for zero-defect food for the manned space programme — astronauts could not risk food poisoning in space — and was first presented publicly by Howard Bauman (Pillsbury's food safety director) at the 1971 National Conference on Food Protection. The system is based on seven principles: identify hazards, determine critical control points (CCPs), establish critical limits, establish monitoring procedures, establish corrective actions, establish verification procedures, and establish documentation.

HACCP represented a revolutionary shift in food safety philosophy — from end-product testing (testing finished food for contamination, which is reactive, statistically limited, and economically wasteful) to process control (identifying the specific points in the production process where hazards can be controlled, monitoring those points, and taking corrective action when critical limits are exceeded). This preventive, process-based approach — with its emphasis on systematic hazard analysis and documented control — proved far more effective at ensuring food safety than the traditional inspection-and-testing model.

HACCP has become the international standard for food safety management — incorporated into the Codex Alimentarius (the UN/WHO international food standards body) in 1993, mandated by the EU for all food businesses from 1995 (Directive 93/43/EEC) and by the US FDA for seafood (1997), meat and poultry, and most recently through the Food Safety Modernization Act (FSMA, 2011).
